content: Antibiotics are occasionally prescribed to prevent recurrent sore throat, although there is concern about the development of antibiotic resistance. However, the evidence regarding their effectiveness in this context is inconsistent. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of antibiotics in patients who experience recurrent sore throat. Recurrent sore throat was defined as having three or more episodes of sore throat within a year. To identify relevant studies, the Cochrane Ear, Nose and Throat Disorders Group (CENTDG) Trials Search Coordinator conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the CENTDG Trials Register, CENTRAL (2015, Issue 5), PubMed, EMBASE, CINAHL, Web of Science, ClinicalTrials.gov, ICTRP, and other sources for both published and unpublished trials. The search was completed on June 25, 2015. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving adults and children with pre-existing recurrent sore throat. These trials needed to assess the incidence of sore throat recurrence and have a follow-up period of at least 12 months after antibiotic therapy. Two authors independently evaluated the quality of the trials and extracted data. Despite multiple attempts to contact the authors of one study, no response was received. No trials met the inclusion criteria for this review. Most references identified during the search were excluded after screening their titles and abstracts. Four studies were formally excluded after reviewing their full-text reports. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to determine whether antibiotics are effective in preventing recurrent sore throat. This lack of evidence must be weighed against the known adverse effects and financial costs associated with antibiotic therapy when considering their use for this purpose. The authors emphasized the need for high-quality randomized controlled trials to compare the effects of antibiotics versus placebo in adults and children with pre-existing recurrent sore throat. These trials should evaluate outcomes such as the recurrence of sore throat, adverse effects, days missed from work or school, and the incidence of complications. Future studies should adhere to the CONSORT (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials) guidelines for proper design and reporting.
